  "text": "The baby monitor began picking up my mother three days after her funeral.

Not her voice. Her cough: two short barks, then the wet rattle she always tried to hide.

We didn’t have a baby. I used the monitor to hear my father if he fell.

“Bad wiring,” he said when I asked.

That evening, I found him unplugging it with oven mitts.

“Don’t answer her,” he told me.

At midnight, the receiver lit up inside my bedside drawer.

“Your father needs his tablets.”

I went downstairs. His pill organizer was empty, though I had filled it that morning.

He watched me from his armchair.

“She used to say that,” he whispered.

The next night, the monitor said his bath was ready.

Water seeped beneath the bathroom door. The taps were running. In the steam, someone had drawn a heart on the mirror, then rubbed it out.

My father packed a suitcase.

“She was ill,” he said. “You know how ill she was.”

I hadn’t asked him anything.

The monitor crackled.

“Tell her which tablets.”

He sat on the suitcase until its lid buckled.

“Tell her how many.”

I looked toward the bathroom. The water had stopped.

For the first time since the funeral, I could smell my mother’s lavender soap.

My father grabbed my wrist.

“Please,” he said. “She asked me to.”

From the receiver came a long, painful effort to breathe.

Then my mother said, quite clearly, “No.”

The bathroom door opened behind him.

I had been holding the monitor’s talk button without realizing it.

“Your bath is ready, Dad,” I said."
